newsitem.title: USA: Net innovations could mean more downsizing -experts.
newsitem.headline: Net innovations could mean more downsizing -experts.

text.p: The World Wide Web's increasing role as a capitalist tool could bring about a new era of corporate downsizing, as companies move toward Internet-based automation methods designed to slash payrolls and other costs, industry executives say.

While the widespread layoffs of recent years continue to spawn job insecurity in the workplace, the computer industry has begun pushing new Web-based software products that allow companies to make some traditional office jobs obsolete.

A leading product line is an Internet-technology called "intranet," which allows companies to set up internal Websites where employees can find up-to-date information about topics such as health and pension plans as well as their employers' latest financial results.

So-called "extranet" products also can be used to create external Internet-links between companies, for the purpose of executing routine business transactions otherwise carried out by paper-based purchase and shipment order systems.

"You can literally remove the people who have been answering the phone in the past. You can remove the paperwork permanently," Bob Herbold, chief operating officer at Microsoft Corp., said in a keynote speech at the Internet Commerce Expo here. "All those phone calls, all those human beings involved, all the paperwork involved can disappear."

A senior executive with International Business Machines Corp. said the government of Singapore was able to reduce manpower by 45 percent and slash costs by 62 percent in some departments after moving suppliers into just such a system.
Meanwhile, computer executives say a cadre of corporations ranging from airlines and automotive companies to consumer product makers and railroads are looking seriously at the potential benefits.

The Internet has yet to overcome the legal, regulatory and security hurdles blocking it from reaching critical mass as a site for electronic commerce. But industry executives remain convinced that it will bring fundamental change to the world economy, possibly in only a few years.

"Just as the Industrial Revolution changed manufacturing capacity, the Internet will change distribution. Middle men and middle-level companies will be eliminated, and most companies in an industrial economy are middle-level," said Shinkhar Ghosh, chairman of the Cambridge, Mass.-based software company Open Market Inc.

But while some experts warn that the Internet could lead to a new period of economic dislocation, others say economic growth resulting from the new way of doing business would more than make up for initial job losses.
"It's less an issue of eliminating jobs than it is an issue of making people more effective," said Randall Whiting, president of the computer industry association CommerceNet.
"There would be so many more business opportunities that overall net employment would rise."
